name: Progressive muscular atrophy
aliases: progressive muscular atrophy variant of motor neurone disease

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive muscle weakness, wasting and fasciculation reflecting pure lower motor neurone degeneration, without upper motor neurone signs
Reflexes are usually reduced or absent and plantar responses are flexor, in contrast to the brisk reflexes of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Weakness is often asymmetrical at onset, commonly beginning in a limb before spreading to other regions
Bulbar and respiratory muscles may become involved as the disease advances, threatening swallowing and breathing
Many patients develop subclinical upper motor neurone or corticospinal pathology over time, so progressive muscular atrophy is regarded as part of the motor neurone disease spectrum
Distinguishing it from treatable lower motor neurone syndromes such as multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block is a diagnostic priority
Care is multidisciplinary and supportive, addressing mobility, communication, nutrition and respiratory function
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive muscular atrophy is a form of motor neurone disease characterised by selective degeneration of the lower motor neurones in the anterior horns of the spinal cord and the motor nuclei of the brainstem, producing denervation, muscle wasting and fasciculation. The corticospinal upper motor neurone pathways are clinically spared, at least initially, distinguishing it from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Post-mortem studies frequently reveal TDP-43 pathology and subclinical corticospinal involvement, supporting the view that progressive muscular atrophy lies at the lower motor neurone end of a continuous motor neurone disease spectrum rather than being a wholly separate entity.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis at an early or lower motor neurone predominant stage
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
Spinal muscular atrophy and other hereditary motor neuronopathies
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with motor predominance
Inclusion body myositis and other myopathies causing wasting
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to confirm widespread denervation and exclude conduction block
MRI of the brain and spine to exclude structural and compressive lesions
Anti-GM1 antibody testing where multifocal motor neuropathy is suspected
Creatine kinase and myopathy screen to exclude a primary muscle disorder
Genetic testing including the androgen receptor gene for Kennedy disease when clinically indicated
Respiratory function testing to monitor for ventilatory involvement
redFlags: Conduction block on nerve conduction studies, suggesting a potentially treatable multifocal motor neuropathy
Emergence of upper motor neurone signs, indicating evolution towards amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Declining respiratory function or nocturnal hypoventilation
Bulbar weakness with unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk
reference.prognosis: Progressive muscular atrophy typically progresses somewhat more slowly than classic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, but many patients develop respiratory and bulbar involvement, and the underlying motor neurone degeneration is ultimately progressive with limited life expectancy in many cases.
pitfalls: Missing multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, a treatable mimic that responds to immunotherapy
Assuming the disorder will remain purely lower motor neurone, when many cases progress within the wider spectrum
Overlooking Kennedy disease, which carries different inheritance and prognosis
Failing to monitor respiratory function until late in the illness
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Disease-modifying therapy with riluzole, as offered across the motor neurone disease spectrum, to modestly slow progression
Respiratory surveillance with regular function testing and non-invasive ventilation for ventilatory insufficiency as respiratory muscles become involved
Nutritional support and dysphagia management, with gastrostomy feeding when swallowing fails
Symptomatic care for cramps, spasticity, sialorrhoea and secretions, with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and mobility and communication aids
Exclude and treat mimics, particularly multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, which responds to intravenous immunoglobulin
Multidisciplinary motor neurone disease clinic care with early palliative care and advance care planning
